The Quiet Art of Reading

By Jane Doe

Reading well is a skill that rewards patience. When the words are set in a comfortable measure, the eye glides without strain, and the mind follows along the line of thought instead of fighting the layout. This first paragraph is long enough to anchor the main content cluster for the extractor to detect reliably.

Typography is not decoration; it is the interface between the reader and the writer. A line that is too long forces the eye to hunt for the start of the next row, and a line that is too short fractures the rhythm of reading. Around sixty-five characters per line is a gentle compromise that typesetters have relied on for centuries.

Colour and contrast

Pure black on pure white vibrates uncomfortably during long sessions. Softer, warmer tones reduce eye strain while preserving accessibility contrast ratios. The goal is calm rather than drama, and the palette should recede so that the words themselves can speak clearly to the reader.

Good design is as little design as possible.

Here is a small code sample, which the reader should preserve verbatim inside a dark code block with monospace text and no smart-quote substitution applied to it:

function greet(name) {
  return "Hello, " + name;
}

The figure below is a simple diagram. In dark mode the reader inverts such images by default, unless the "keep figures light" option is enabled by the reader.

A closing paragraph rounds out the body so that the article remains the dominant column of prose on the page and the extractor locks onto it without ambiguity or drift.
